central_finding: A distinct article can explain changing meanings of Khandayat, the connection between fort settlement and cultivation, historically disputed boundaries with Chasa, and locally documented domestic heritage. Evidence does not establish one caste founder or date of creation. Khurda evidence must not become a genealogy of every Khandayat family.

sources.title: Akio Tanabe, Genealogies of the ‘Paika Rebellion’: Heterogeneities and Linkages
sources.publication: International Journal of Asian Studies 17(1), 2020, pp.1–18; DOI 10.1017/S1479591420000157
sources.inspection: Full original publisher HTML previously inspected for Paika and re-used for this research.
sources.locator: Paragraph beginning ‘In the precolonial period, various inhabitants…’ and following paragraphs on hereditary positions and Puri census, HTML lines582–592; late18c pay records around574.
sources.claims: Service positions, with land or pay, could become hereditary. Census returns discussed by Tanabe record Khandayats in Puri district increasing from 8,193 in 1891 to 112,571 in 1931 while Chasas decrease from 273,715 to 231,021. He interprets changing identification and status claims, not a biological population transformation. This is evidence against projecting fixed present-day boundaries backwards; it does not equate all Chasas with Khandayats or all Paikas with either community.
sources.strength: Peer-reviewed historical anthropology using archival records and ethnography; census interpretation is the author's argument.
limits: Do not reproduce erroneous62/291=23.7% calculation elsewhere in article.
Numbers describe a particular district and categories of enumeration, not all Odisha or present population.

sources.title: Akio Tanabe, Managing diversities: Frontiers, forest communities and little kingdoms
sources.publication: Chapter2, Caste and Equality in India: A Historical Anthropology of Diverse Society and Vernacular Democracy, pp25–43, Routledge copyright/first-published2022 edition; DOI10.4324/9781003173519-2. ResearchGate metadata says July2021, author upload September2022; cite edition, not upload date.
sources.inspection: Author-uploaded full-text HTML inspected. Some embedded-font lines garbled; opening page25 fully legible. No accessible downloaded PDF obtained.
sources.locator: p25 opening; pp35–36 ‘Existing polities and emerging fort areas’, HTML809–862.
sources.claims: For Khurda kingdom (c1570–1804), Tanabe describes forts in forest clearings, villages and fields around them, managed water and grazing, and forest-dwellers becoming warriors, cultivators and herdsmen alongside newcomers from the plains. The kingdom's dates are not a caste birthdate. In discussing early chiefs he distinguishes khandayata as autonomous chief from caste name. A Saori Khandayat origin story collected by him links a Gajapati king, Saora woman and thirteen sons. Present it only as a locally narrated claim joining royal and Saora origins, never proof of descent or a dated foundation.
sources.strength: Original scholarly historical anthropology with author-collected traditions and cited historical records; oral narrative is evidence of memory, not verification of the narrated event.
limits: Scope is principally Khurda frontier formation.
Opening environmental account supports precise landscape illustration; chief terminology/origin passage has partial font corruption and deserves independent visual review if quoted exactly.
Do not repeat purity/rank terminology as objective human value.

sources.title: Jogendra Nath Bhattacharya, Hindu Castes and Sects
sources.locator: PDF171–172, printed147–148; p147 visually inspected in /tmp/pod-bhat-page171.png
sources.claims: The author glosses Khandait as swordsman and distinguishes Mahanayaka/Sreshta from Paik or Chasa Khandaits, while describing movement toward agriculture. His listed titles include Jena, Nayaka, Rout, Samanta and Senapati. Useful as a dated witness to nineteenth-century classification and attempts to relate cultivation, military office and identity. Neither the author's military ancestry explanation nor his social ranking establishes every family's origin. A surname alone cannot verify an ancestor's office.
sources.strength: Original colonial-era text by an Indian author; historical witness to categorisation, not modern ethnography or independently established genealogy.
limits: Do not universalise its branches or marriage descriptions to contemporary Odisha.
Reject its purity, race and rank assumptions; use restrained explicit date/author attribution.

sources.title: Yumiko Tokita-Tanabe, Women and Tradition in India: Construction of Subjectivity and Control of Female Sexuality in the Ritual of First Menstruation
sources.locator: Printed198–200 domestic responsibilities/household offerings;205(PDF14) turmeric and oil bathing;214 note1(PDF23) fieldwork scope.
sources.claims: Fieldwork ran April1991–November1992 among Khandayat women in Garh Manitri, Khurda. It documents household and ancestral offerings prepared by women, including food and water, revealing heritage beyond martial office. It also records turmeric and oil in a puberty bathing ritual. Thus turmeric itself cannot simply be dismissed as absent from local tradition; this source does not establish the antiquity or provenance of today's staged wedding Haldi ceremony. Keep ritual setting, village and dates explicit, without intimate details or a claim of uniform present practice.
sources.strength: Original ethnographic fieldwork, precisely dated and located.
limits: One village, one fieldwork period; not a survey of all branches or contemporary2026 practice.
Gender hierarchy is analysed by author, not endorsed as required heritage.
Turmeric evidence concerns puberty, not weddings.

narrative_plan.content: Start with swordsman gloss as a dated interpretation, then ask how service, fields and family identity became connected. No single creator established.
Explain settlement, water, grazing, crops and recruited skills in early-modern Khurda; distinguish kingdom chronology from caste creation.

narrative_plan.section: A name that changed its boundaries
narrative_plan.content: Inherited service positions and changing Puri census identification; explain why Chasa relationship cannot be reduced to simple permanent equivalence.
Nineteenth-century distinctions explicitly as author taxonomy; very brief Saori origin-story example as memory, with no literal descent claim.
Dated village women's contributions, turmeric documented in its actual ritual context and limitation of wedding inference.
Regional family records, local usage and consent-based oral history remain needed; no exhaustive regional genealogy claimed.
